questions.prompt: Regular hexagons are inscribed in and circumscribed about a circle of radius 1. Their perimeters are 6 and 4√3 ≈ 6.93. Explain why this shows that 3 < π < 2√3 ≈ 3.46.
questions.prompt_markup: Regular hexagons are inscribed in and circumscribed about a circle of radius 1. Their perimeters are 6 and 4√3 ≈ 6.93. Explain why this shows that 3 < π < 2√3 ≈ 3.46.
questions.correct_answer: The circle lies between the two hexagons, so 6 < C < 4√3; with C = 2π this gives 3 < π < 2√3 ≈ 3.46.
questions.required_method: Compare the circumference 2π with the two perimeters, then divide by 2.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the inscribed hexagon is six equilateral triangles of side 1 (perimeter 6); the circumference is between the inner and outer perimeters; C = 2π · 1; divide by 2. Invalid: quoting π ≈ 3.14 as the reason.

questions.prompt: Explain why the ratio of circumference to diameter is the same number (π) for every circle, so that C = πd = 2πr.
questions.prompt_markup: Explain why the ratio of circumference to diameter is the same number (π) for every circle, so that C = πd = 2πr.
questions.correct_answer: Every circle is a dilation of every other, so C and d scale by the same factor and C/d is constant; that constant is called π.
questions.required_method: Use the fact that all circles are similar.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: circles are similar (dilation); lengths scale by the same factor k; C₂/d₂ = kC₁/kd₁ = C₁/d₁.

questions.prompt: A wheel with diameter 70 cm rolls one full turn along level ground without slipping, and a student measures the distance traveled as 219.9 cm. Explain why that distance is the circumference, use the measurement to estimate π, and say why a measurement supports the formula but does not prove it.
questions.prompt_markup: A wheel with diameter 70 cm rolls one full turn along level ground without slipping, and a student measures the distance traveled as 219.9 cm. Explain why that distance is the circumference, use the measurement to estimate π, and say why a measurement supports the formula but does not prove it.
questions.correct_answer: Each point of the rim touches the ground once in one turn, so the distance equals the circumference; 219.9 ÷ 70 ≈ 3.141, close to π. A measurement has error and covers one wheel only.
questions.required_method: Relate each point of the rim to the ground it touches; divide distance by diameter.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: rolling without slipping lays the rim along the ground; C/d ≈ 3.141; evidence versus proof.

questions.prompt: Regular polygons with 6, 12 and 24 sides are inscribed in a circle of radius 1. Their perimeters are 6, 6.212 and 6.265. Explain what these values suggest about the circumference and how the formula C = 2πr follows for a circle of any radius r.
questions.prompt_markup: Regular polygons with 6, 12 and 24 sides are inscribed in a circle of radius 1. Their perimeters are 6, 6.212 and 6.265. Explain what these values suggest about the circumference and how the formula C = 2πr follows for a circle of any radius r.
questions.correct_answer: The perimeters increase toward 2π ≈ 6.283, the circumference of the unit circle; a circle of radius r is the unit circle dilated by r, so its circumference is 2π · r.
questions.required_method: Describe the trend of the perimeters, then use similarity (scaling by r).
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the inscribed perimeters approach the circumference from below; the limit for radius 1 is 2π; dilation by r multiplies lengths by r.

questions.prompt: Use the circumference formula to explain why an arc with central angle 90° in a circle of radius 6 has length 3π, and find its length to the nearest tenth.
questions.prompt_markup: Use the circumference formula to explain why an arc with central angle 90° in a circle of radius 6 has length 3π, and find its length to the nearest tenth.
questions.correct_answer: The arc is 90/360 = ¼ of the circle, so its length is ¼ · 2π · 6 = 3π ≈ 9.4.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the fraction-of-the-circle reasoning and the value (rounding to 0.1).
